items.title: Montée des océans : Une menace croissante pour les populations, les cultures et les États
items.description: La hausse du niveau des mers n’est plus seulement un enjeu environnemental. Selon un récent rapport relayé par ONU Info, elle pourrait bouleverser des sociétés entières, fragiliser la souveraineté de certains États et effacer des pans entiers du patrimoine culturel mondial. Derrière les chiffres du réchauffement climatique se profile ainsi une crise humaine, juridique et identitaire d’une ampleur inédite, susceptible de contraindre près de 1,2 milliard de personnes à migrer d’ici à 2050 pour trouver des territoires plus sûrs et de nouvelles sources de revenus. Le phénomène s’accélère à un rythme sans précédent sous l’effet des activités humaines responsables du changement climatique. Entre 2014 et 2023, le niveau moyen des océans a progressé de 4,7 millimètres par an à l’échelle mondiale, avant d’atteindre un record de 5,9 millimètres en 2024. Les projections les plus optimistes tablent sur une hausse de 55 centimètres d’ici à 2100, tandis que les scénarios les plus pessimistes envisagent une élévation supérieure à un mètre. Dans l’hypothèse d’une poursuite des fortes émissions de gaz à effet de serre, la montée des eaux pourrait même approcher les deux mètres à la fin du siècle. Cette progression résulte principalement de la fonte des glaciers et des calottes glaciaires, mais également de la dilatation thermique des océans. En absorbant près de 91 % de l’excès de chaleur accumulé sur la planète, les masses océaniques se réchauffent et occupent davantage d’espace. Une dynamique qui rend inévitables de nouvelles augmentations du niveau marin, même si les émissions venaient à ralentir. Les conséquences se font déjà sentir dans les zones côtières. Quelque 770 millions de personnes, soit près d’un habitant sur dix dans le monde, vivent dans des régions littorales de faible altitude particulièrement exposées. La salinisation des nappes phréatiques et des terres agricoles, la multiplication des inondations et la dégradation d’infrastructures essentielles – hôpitaux, écoles ou réseaux d’assainissement – figurent parmi les effets les plus visibles. À cela s’ajoutent une hausse des maladies liées à l’eau ainsi que les perturbations qui frappent les secteurs de la pêche et du tourisme, piliers économiques de nombreuses régions côtières. Au-delà des dommages matériels, la montée des eaux menace également des patrimoines culturels parfois irremplaçables. Les Nations unies alertent sur le risque de disparition de territoires ancestraux, de sites historiques et de savoirs traditionnels étroitement liés aux espaces côtiers. Pour certaines communautés, notamment autochtones ou insulaires, la perte de terres signifie aussi celle d’une mémoire collective, d’une identité culturelle et de modes de vie transmis depuis des générations. Le coût économique de cette crise s’annonce colossal. Les dommages déjà enregistrés sur les infrastructures côtières dépassent 1.800 milliards de dollars. Sans politiques d’adaptation, les pertes annuelles mondiales pourraient atteindre 1.400 milliards de dollars. Les petits États insulaires en développement ont, à eux seuls, subi des pertes estimées à 153 milliards de dollars entre 1970 et 2020. Aux États-Unis, les primes d’assurance habitation ont progressé de 33 % entre 2020 et 2023 sous l’effet de l’aggravation des risques climatiques. Les ports, par lesquels transite plus de 80 % du commerce mondial, figurent également parmi les infrastructures les plus vulnérables. Les disparités géographiques sont particulièrement marquées. Les petites îles du Pacifique apparaissent parmi les territoires les plus exposés, avec une élévation du niveau de la mer dépassant parfois deux fois la moyenne mondiale. Les grandes métropoles situées dans des deltas de faible altitude, comme Dacca, Mumbai ou Kolkata, sont également en première ligne. Plus de 14 millions de personnes y sont menacées de perdre leur logement, voire leur vie. Des villes côtières majeures telles que Miami, New York ou Guangzhou sont elles aussi confrontées à des risques croissants. Les scientifiques surveillent par ailleurs avec inquiétude le glacier Thwaites, en Antarctique. S’étendant sur près de 190 000 kilomètres carrés, cette immense masse de glace pourrait, en cas d’effondrement, provoquer une hausse soudaine et irréversible du niveau des mers supérieure à un demi-mètre. Face à cette perspective, les Nations unies plaident pour une réduction rapide de la dépendance aux énergies fossiles afin de freiner le réchauffement climatique. Elles appellent également à renforcer les politiques d’adaptation : systèmes d’alerte précoce, digues maritimes, restauration des mangroves, réhabilitation des dunes côtières ou encore programmes de relocalisation planifiée des populations les plus exposées. La clarification du statut juridique des États et de leurs espaces maritimes en cas de submersion figure également parmi les priorités identifiées. Reste la question du financement. Les pays en développement auraient besoin de mobiliser entre 310 et 365 milliards de dollars par an pour s’adapter aux effets du changement climatique. Pourtant, les financements mondiaux consacrés à cet objectif n’ont atteint que 26 milliards de dollars en 2023. Pour les Nations unies, combler cet écart constitue désormais une urgence, au même titre que la protection des populations, des territoires et des patrimoines menacés par l’avancée inexorable des océans. The post Montée des océans : Une menace croissante pour les populations, les cultures et les États appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Hegseth’s Pentagon Lurches off the Rails
items.description: Making Pete Hegseth the secretary of defense was always a huge gamble. A television host with little background in national-security or defense affairs, who topped out as a major in the National Guard, he was nominated based on the same qualification shared by most of Donald Trump’s other appointees: loyalty. And now the price of that gamble is evident. The Pentagon is careening offtrack under a secretary of defense who is firing or forcing the resignations of officers and civilian officials, not because they are unqualified but because he believes they are insufficiently loyal to him, personally. The latest casualty of Hegseth’s ongoing purge is Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who resigned today after repeatedly clashing with the secretary of defense. As my colleagues Nancy A. Youssef, Missy Ryan, and Michael Scherer report , a person familiar with Driscoll’s resignation said that he had “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible.” In the careful circumlocutions of Washington-speak, that means that Driscoll went to the White House to complain about Hegseth, and the president sided with Hegseth. But more issues were in play than “Army transformation.” Hegseth’s tenure has been disastrous on multiple scores. Instead of giving sound advice to the commander in chief and ensuring that America remains secure while the president fights a deeply unwise war of choice, he has been pursuing his political grievances about DEI and other pet peeves against the U.S. military. Hegseth seems to have a special animus toward the Army, an institution he claims “spit me out.” He fired Army Chief of Staff General Randy George, and he has pushed out other senior Army officers; at this point, the Army has no Senate-confirmed chief of staff or secretary. (George’s replacement, General Christopher LaNeve, so far does not have the necessary votes to be confirmed.) Even in less dangerous times, Hegseth’s irresponsible behavior would be a hazard to American national security. The Defense Department is a huge bureaucracy; it requires a leader who understands more than the mechanics of teaching trainees how to do push-ups or how to handle a weapon. Secretaries of defense must grasp the economics of the defense industry, the nature of alliances, congressional politics, the policy process, and dozens of other issues for which Hegseth seems to care little and about which he knows even less. In a time of war, however, Hegseth’s shortcomings may prove deadly. Leave aside his early stumbles, including the mishandling of sensitive information . Leave aside, even, that Hegseth dissembled about the severity of Iranian attacks on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf that had succeeded in disrupting the logistical support for American forces in the theater and led to the kind of deprivations that were suffered by the crew of the aircraft carrier the USS Abraham Lincoln. Hegseth’s incompetence, and his commitment to staying in Trump’s good graces, helped launch the war itself in the first place. Hegseth was reportedly virtually alone among senior officials in supporting Trump’s decision to attack Iran—when he should have been the one person in the room who knew better. The secretary of state and CIA director were against the idea. According to the The Wall Street Journal , even then–Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, another of Trump’s unqualified-but-sycophantic appointees, mustered the courage to give the president bad news, telling Trump that killing the reigning ayatollah and striking Iran would “likely usher in a more hard-line regime open to acquiring nuclear weapons”; that the Iranians “would rush to close the Strait of Hormuz, destabilizing the global energy market”; and that Iran “would strike U.S. forces and partners in the Middle East,” all of which happened almost immediately after Trump gave the order to go to war. Hegseth, however, supported Trump’s fantasies of a quick victory. A man of principle would have warned his president even at the risk of his job, but Pete Hegseth is not that man. And now Hegseth has banished another enemy, Driscoll, from the Pentagon. But as the saying goes: Play stupid games, win stupid prizes. Hegseth, more than ever, now owns every aspect of the Pentagon’s dysfunction. Yesterday, The Washington Post reported that multiple senior military leaders—those still left, that is—have warned Hegseth that the United States cannot indefinitely extend military operations against Iran. Even the chief of naval operations, Admiral Darryl Caudle (who campaigned for the job by signaling his agreement with the secretary’s culture-war obsessions), told Hegseth that the Navy cannot “sustain its current level of support for the Iran conflict because there is no anticipated end date.” Hegseth’s response to this story was to send his spokespeople out to castigate the press for revealing classified information. In an amateurish bungle, the Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said that the reports were “inaccurate” but also a “betrayal of the force”—leading sensible people to ask how the stories could be false and dangerous at the same time. And these were just the responses from people who are officially authorized to speak for the Pentagon; another bombshell report over the weekend revealed that the department has recruited online influencers into paid roles, but without either the influencers or the Pentagon telling anyone about their cozy arrangement with the government. Hegseth, meanwhile, has dutifully overseen the raiding of assets from other theaters to support Trump’s war with Iran, leaving the U.S. and its allies exposed to potential threats from China and Russia. When Trump returned to office, Hegseth and others supported a reorientation away from the Middle East and Europe. Now the secretary and the other supposed China hawks have discarded those positions and dumped everything into a war that still has no clear strategy and no clear goal beyond stopping Iran from attaining a nuclear weapon it didn’t have in the first place. Fortunately, even under the strain of a petty and incompetent secretary, and a president mired in his delusions, senior military officers are still speaking up and telling their boss the truth about America’s parlous defense situation. One of the advantages of a large bureaucracy staffed with professionals is that much of it can run and function, at least for a while, under even the most inept leaders. But Hegseth is apparently close to getting the Pentagon he wants: Much like his boss at the White House, Hegseth seems to desire a building full of loyalists who put the boss’s personal fortunes over the national interest. Some reports indicate , for example, that Hegseth wants to replace Driscoll with Parnell—who has no significant qualifications for the post beyond his time fighting with the press on the secretary’s behalf. The result of all this is that the United States is losing a war to a third-rate power in the Middle East. The Russians, meanwhile, are continuing their rampage in Europe and apparently considering things so perilous that the CIA director had to fly to Moscow just to warn the Kremlin off of whatever it was thinking of doing. The Chinese are watching as Trump and Hegseth have stripped the Pacific theater of its only American aircraft carrier. In the midst of this chaos, Hegseth does chin-ups while he ponders calling all of America’s admirals and generals back to another mass meeting so he can again carp at them about fat soldiers and bearded sailors. Pete Hegseth has failed in every mission except one: keeping his job. But firing or forcing out everyone else in the Pentagon will not make Pete Hegseth into the secretary of defense America and its men and women in uniform need. With each dismissal, he exposes only his own insecurities, even as he manages to stay employed—but the people and the armed forces of the United States are paying the inevitable price of his incompetence.

items.title: Maladie de Alzheimer : découverte d’un déclencheur précoce dans le cerveau par des scientifiques américains
items.description: La maladie d’Alzheimer pourrait débuter bien plus tôt que ce qui était admis jusqu’alors par la communauté médicale. Selon des données rapportées par la rédaction de Science & Vie et publiées en août 2026 dans la revue spécialisée Science , une modification cellulaire majeure survient parfois dès la cinquantaine. Ce processus biologique invisible s’enclenche des dizaines d’années avant que les premiers symptômes de perte de mémoire ou de désorientation n’apparaissent lors des bilans cliniques. Cette découverte remet en question la chronologie traditionnelle de la maladie en identifiant une phase initiale particulièrement précoce. Ces travaux ont été conduits par des chercheurs de l’Université de Californie à San Diego, sous la direction du chercheur Nathan Zemke, qui ont cherché à comprendre les dérèglements microcellulaires associés au vieillissement cérébral. Une analyse approfondie de l’hippocampe et du génome credit : lanature.ca (image IA) Pour analyser ces manifestations précoces, l’équipe scientifique américaine s’est concentrée sur l’hippocampe, la structure cérébrale centrale impliquée dans les processus de mémorisation. Les analyses ont été effectuées sur les tissus de 40 adultes dont l’âge s’échelonnait entre 20 et 95 ans. Afin d’obtenir une vue précise des mécanismes en jeu, les scientifiques ont croisé plusieurs paramètres biologiques complexes. Ils ont combiné la mesure de l’activité génétique, l’étude de la structure tridimensionnelle du génome et l’analyse des marques épigénétiques au niveau des cellules cérébrales. Même si le vieillissement naturel demeure le principal facteur de risque associé au développement d’Alzheimer, la séquence exacte des altérations initiales demeurait mal comprise avant cette étude. Le remplacement des microglies par des cellules sanguines credit : credit : lanature.ca (image IA) L’observation clé des scientifiques repose sur un changement de population cellulaire au cœur du cerveau. À partir de 50 ans, les microglies, qui sont les cellules immunitaires natives du cerveau, commencent à être progressivement remplacées par des cellules provenant du système sanguin. Ces cellules candidates présentent la signature biologique des monocytes sanguins. Une fois installées dans le tissu cérébral, elles génèrent une production accrue de signaux inflammatoires au niveau de l’hippocampe. Cette réaction inflammatoire s’installe progressivement et précède de plusieurs décennies le déclin cognitif observable, agissant comme un déclencheur à bas bruit au sein de l’organisme. Altération de la barrière hémato-encéphalique et dérégulation globale credit : lanature.ca (image IA) L’impact de ce remplacement cellulaire ne se limite pas à la sécrétion de signaux inflammatoires. L’étude révèle que les cellules maintenant la barrière hémato-encéphalique, chargée de protéger le cerveau des agents toxiques, subissent un affaiblissement notable à la même période. Parallèlement, les chercheurs observent une baisse du nombre d’astrocytes ainsi qu’une désorganisation tridimensionnelle du génome à travers divers types cellulaires. L’ensemble de ces phénomènes témoigne d’une perte progressive de la régulation biologique globale dans le cerveau. Ces constats apportent un éclairage nouveau sur une statistique critique soulignée par l’étude : près de 42 % des Américains de plus de 55 ans seraient susceptibles de développer une forme de démence au cours de leur existence. Perspectives thérapeutiques et vidéo explicative credit : credit : lanature.ca (image IA) L’identification de ce mécanisme précoce ouvre de nouvelles perspectives pour la prévention. Les auteurs de l’étude suggèrent qu’il pourrait être possible d’élaborer des traitements visant à freiner la migration des cellules sanguines vers le cerveau ou à préserver plus longtemps les microglies natives afin d’empêcher l’apparition des troubles de la mémoire. Ces pistes prometteuses doivent encore faire l’objet de confirmations lors de travaux ultérieurs sur des échantillons de population plus vastes. Il est possible de consulter un contenu complémentaire via cette explication vidéo sur l’origine de la maladie d’Alzheimer. Pour toute question médicale, consultez un professionnel de santé qualifié. Selon la source : passeportsante.net L’article Maladie de Alzheimer : découverte d’un déclencheur précoce dans le cerveau par des scientifiques américains est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Dan Driscoll’s Parting Shot
items.description: D uring a White House meeting last week , Army Secretary Dan Driscoll brought his concerns about the future of the Army under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directly to President Trump—a sign of how far tensions between the two Pentagon leaders had escalated, and of the dysfunction inside the building, four people familiar with the conversation told us. Trump was surprised when Driscoll told him how many generals and other top officers had been fired, pushed out, or passed over for promotion under Hegseth, one of the people said. Driscoll argued that the Army could not transform itself the way it needs to, because of the departure of so many leaders, this person said, adding that Trump expressed concern about the deep cuts to the Army’s senior leadership. Driscoll informed the president of his intention to resign—and by today, Driscoll was on his way out. Hegseth’s purge of the military has been so dramatic that with Driscoll gone, the military’s largest service is left without a top civilian leader, a Senate-confirmed top general, a confirmed Army general in charge of operations, or a confirmed commander of Army troops in Europe. Because of all the firings across the service over the past year, the Army, with more than 450,000 active-duty soldiers positioned across the globe, has fewer generals than at any point in recent history. Driscoll’s personal appeal to Trump just days before his exit was the most direct articulation of high-level concerns among Pentagon leaders about the strains facing the force—including Hegseth’s intervention in Army personnel decisions and the mounting demands of the Iran war. The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that Driscoll had been “highly effective” in improving soldier readiness and advancing other administration priorities. “The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” Kelly wrote in a statement, using the administration’s preferred term for the Department of Defense. Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment, and Driscoll did not respond to a call seeking comment. But a person familiar with his resignation told us that Driscoll had “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible.” Hegseth did not have an immediate response to Driscoll’s departure. [ Read: The military Pete Hegseth wants ] Since his arrival at the Pentagon early last year, Hegseth—a former Fox News host who appealed to Trump loyalists by deriding a “woke” military and advocating for leniency for troops charged with war crimes—has sought to reshape the Army. He has placed like-minded generals in positions of influence, intervened to stymie the promotions of lower ranking-officers, and gutted diversity initiatives. The result was an Army depleted of leaders, and an Army secretary and a Pentagon chief at constant odds. Hegseth has ended dozens of Army careers, all without any clear explanation. He now has driven out the secretary of the Army. Driscoll’s departure puts the Pentagon even more firmly under the control of Hegseth and his MAGA agenda. Driscoll is a confidant of Vice President Vance, a relationship that gave him access to the West Wing, and at times Driscoll served as a counterweight to Hegseth’s impulses, but only up to a point. Some current and former defense officials told us they believe Driscoll’s enmity toward Hegseth actually had the unintended consequence of broadening the purge of the uniformed ranks. And yet Driscoll’s departure, which had been expected for months, and the prospect that he will be replaced by someone more politically aligned with Hegseth are already raising fears inside the Army. “What happens then? Generational damage,” a defense official told us. D riscoll arrived at the Pentagon in February 2025, a third-generation Army soldier who shared several things in common with Hegseth, his new boss. Like Hegseth, Driscoll joined the military in the most muscular years of Washington’s post-9/11 wars. Both men served in Iraq in a company-grade role. (Hegseth, a National Guardsman, also deployed to Afghanistan.) Both returned with sharp criticisms of America’s overseas adventures and the military’s hidebound ways. Both attended Ivy League schools: Hegseth, Princeton and Harvard; Driscoll, Yale Law, where he befriended the fellow veteran Vance. Both Driscoll and Hegseth have made unsuccessful runs for political office. Both have also eyed a return to politics. As Army secretary, Driscoll frequently reminded people that he had a direct line to the vice president, people familiar with the matter said, and told others that he had ambition to someday run for president himself—an ambition that Hegseth is also said to harbor. But the two men differed starkly in temperament and style. Hegseth, who required an unprecedented tie-breaking Senate-confirmation vote from Vance after failing to win any Democratic support, is one of Trump’s most reliable MAGA warriors. He has publicly boasted about firing “woke” generals, dared military dissenters to quit, and demonized the mainstream media. Driscoll also supported administration policies but has done so in a more genial way that appealed to many lawmakers more than Hegseth’s combative approach before Congress. And unlike Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who has echoed Hegseth’s scornful and partisan tone on social media, Driscoll has steered clear of endorsing Hegseth’s most controversial actions or most of his culture-war priorities. Unlike Hegseth, Driscoll is friendly with the press, cultivated ties with lawmakers of both parties, and courted technology leaders as he promoted the Army’s sprint to transform how it wages war. That served him well in the administration, earning him additional responsibilities as director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and later as an unofficial mediator for the war in Ukraine. None of that sat well with Hegseth. Army personnel appointments were a particular point of friction. Hegseth has not hesitated to push aside or promote officers as he sees fit, in many cases in ways that have irked others in the Pentagon. Driscoll advocated for General Randy George, the Army chief of staff whose name appeared on a list circulated before Trump’s return to office of senior officers who should be fired due to perceived transgressions against the MAGA agenda. Although Driscoll may have bought George time, Hegseth ultimately fired the general in April. Chris Donahue, the four-star general who headed U.S. Army Europe and Africa, followed several months later. T he Army has been without a top commander since George’s firing. General Christopher LaNeve, who was picked by Hegseth as the No. 2 officer in the Army, has been acting in that role, often going straight to Hegseth for decisions, bypassing Driscoll, according to defense officials. Hegseth is expected to nominate LaNeve to lead the Army, but Capitol Hill is already signaling that LaNeve would struggle to be confirmed, because of many lawmakers’ antipathy to Hegseth. “We are not going to reward Hegseth for what he did to the Army,” one congressional staffer told us. [ Read: Americans deserve answers from Hegseth ] The Army has long prided itself on representing the diversity of the country, but under Hegseth, minorities and women have been pushed out or barred from promotion. The military has long sought to be apolitical, but under Hegseth, troops are measured not by combat experience but by their perceived loyalty to the administration. Among the generals fired have been some of the most experienced and decorated in the service. Each departure marks the loss of decades of investment in that soldier and raises questions about how future troops can rise through the ranks. Although Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal is expected to take over in the near term, many Pentagon officials fear that the administration will nominate the Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, another Army veteran, to replace Driscoll. Parnell, who previously made a failed bid for U.S. Senate in Pennsylvania, shares Hegseth’s pugilistic spirit and interest in culture and personnel issues. Like Hegseth, Parnell has no experience managing a large organization and would face a contentious confirmation hearing. A new Army secretary who is more politically driven—and likely less experienced and less well connected than Driscoll—could keep the service embroiled in cultural fights rather than focused on the long-term planning that Driscoll and others believe it desperately needs.

items.title: Trump’s Economy Goes to the Polls
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Midterm elections are almost always referendums on the policies of the party in power; President Trump is hoping that Republicans steer into the skid. Last week, my colleagues reported that the president—dogged by the war in Iran, the trade war with Canada, and an economy that has Americans dipping into their savings for groceries and daily expenses—hopes that Republicans seeking to win reelection or gain seats will use his time in office to sway voters. But that strategy could play directly into the hands of Democrats hoping to take back both chambers of Congress. My colleagues the Atlantic staff writers Michael Scherer and Ashley Parker join me this week to discuss Congress, the economy, and the midterm elections. The following is a transcript of the episode: Ashley Parker: At the end of the day, one thing that President Trump is great at is getting people to sort of remember and understand what it is he ostensibly cares about, right? Whether that’s “Drain the Swamp” or Space Force. And Democrats need to find a way to signal—need an elevator pitch that voters can say, I’m voting for the Democrats because I know that my interest rate will go down to 3.875 percent . [ Music ] Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic . I’m Adam Harris, and this week, we need to think about the midterms. The House of Representatives is back on Capitol Hill this week as the nation turns its attention to the general election. It’s the last opportunity for lawmakers to show they are working for their constituents. Meanwhile, President Trump is trying to convince congressional Republicans to run on his record. But amid a war with Iran driving up the price of everyday items and a burgeoning trade war with Canada, Americans are feeling the pinch of the president’s agenda. And Democrats, on the heel of bitter primary races around the country, are hoping to seize upon the president’s unpopularity, and they’re banking that Americans want something different. The question is: Are they right? I’m joined by my colleagues Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer to discuss. Ashley, Michael, welcome to the show. Michael Scherer: Thanks for having us. Parker: Thanks for having us. Harris: Ashley, I want to start with you first. Congress is back this week, and one of the first things that they must do is to fund the government, right? Do you think that Congress is more likely to get this done in a timely manner than we’ve seen in some of these previous spending cycles? Parker: Yeah, I mean, a lot of these stopgap measures end up being incredibly fraught and going up to the last minute. This one is looking like it’s going to be less controversial, in part because what House members really wanna do is get back to their districts to campaign for the midterms. And so there’s a few things in there that might raise some eyebrows, but the sense right now is that they’ll be able to, they hope, push this through pretty quickly. Harris: Speaking of kind of getting back to the districts for the midterms, right, this is a very important cycle. I feel like every cycle we say, It’s, you know — Scherer: — most important election of your lifetime . Harris: Exactly. The most important one of the lifetime. But this one is a pretty important cycle, particularly for Democrats hoping to stop the president’s agenda and for Republicans hoping to continue with the president’s policies moving forward. Oftentimes, parties don’t like to make this a referendum on the presidency. I’m reminded of [Barack] Obama saying, I’m not on the ballot, but these policies are certainly on the ballot . And you both have reported that Trump is planning to roll out a series of TV ads that are touting his personal record leading up to the midterms in November. What does this ad blitz say about the administration and how they’re feeling about the election prospects, Michael, and the president’s image? Scherer: Yeah, so there’s a formula for midterm elections. It’s always a referendum on those in power. So the in-party—the people who hold the presidency, and if they also hold the House, the Senate—try their best to make it a choice, not a referendum, to basically put the opposing party in the spotlight, say, Look, they’re terrible and bad and have done all these awful things, and if you give them back power, it’ll be terrible . And they’re always fighting an uphill battle, because voters don’t see it that way, and voters tend to just, you know, say, I’m happy or I’m pissed off . And you know, for the last four decades, they’re almost always pissed off when it comes to a midterm. This cycle is a little different because of voting patterns and the appeal of President Trump. [It] used to be that Republicans turned out more than Democrats in midterms. Now that’s kind of reversed. Democrats are more likely to turn out in midterms. [It] used to be that presidents don’t really have much impact on who turns out in midterms, for the reasons I just said—you know, it’s a referendum, and people are upset. Republicans are betting on this idea that their biggest problem is motivation, that they have the voters out there, that if they can get those voters to the polls, they can stem their losses, they could actually overperform expectations. But the polls right now show, you know, they’re not that excited. Like, a Fox News poll a few weeks ago asked, Are you extremely motivated to vote? Democrat voters were like 70 percent saying they’re extremely motivated; Republican voters, like 60 percent saying they were extremely motivated. And so the White House solution to that, the president’s solution to that, is to say, We’ve got the magic man on the stump here. We’re going to make this about President Trump , which really undermines the pattern I just described. You know, the Republicans and the Democrats now are in some way saying, We’re gonna make this a referendum on the president . Parker: And to be clear, everything is always about President Trump. That’s just the rule of President Trump. And so as much as this strategy that Michael and I and our colleague Yvonne reported last week seems counterintuitive and is legitimately frustrating to some Republicans, the White House thinking and the president’s thinking is, It’s always about Trump , right? And he likes it being about himself, and so if it’s gonna be about him, we might as well put him front and center and tout what we believe are his accomplishments . Harris: Yeah, if he’s gonna be there, why run away from him? Might as well steer into the skid, right? Scherer: The problem is that the more you’re talking about Trump and trying to convince people that he’s, you know, improved everyone’s lives when the polls show people don’t feel like he’s improved their lives in the last year and a half, the less you’re talking about Democrats. And so, you know, that’s the choice they’re making. It’s not that it’s a terrible idea to be talking about the president. You know, another pattern is, like, Obama would go out on the stump and, you know, [Joe] Biden went on the stump in his midterm elections, [George W. ] Bush went on the stump in his midterm elections, and would obviously talk about their own records. So it’s not like presidents don’t talk about themselves. The difference here is putting money on TV and digital media about the president. Normally, the in-party only wants to talk about how terrible and bad the out-party is. And, you know, that’s especially true for super PACs. The president’s talking about spending. He’s got $400 million we know about. He may have hundreds of millions more in sort of dark money, basically independent money he’s collected. Normally, that money is just used to ravage the other side and just tear them apart. And the idea that the president’s gonna put some significant part of that behind convincing people that no tax on tips, or the stock-market highs, or the closed border have really done them well is what’s so controversial. Harris: And how are congressional Republicans feeling about this? How have they sort of responded to the president trying to have his name sort of be more forward in the campaign? Parker: In general, if they’re speaking candidly, which they don’t really do in public, because they’re fearful of the blowback from President Trump, they find him generally unhelpful in this moment, right? A lot of the things he says and does just further the sense that he and his party don’t care about voters like them. So there’s some stuff he said. He was recently at a rally in South Carolina for Darline Graham, Lindsay Graham’s sister, who’s running to replace him, where he said, I know my economic numbers are bad, but they should actually be at 100 percent. I’m doing such a great job . That makes people—who, you know, are going to maybe two or three grocery stores right now to use their coupons to get the best deals on what they can—feel like, He has no idea what my life is like . That’s, like, a very clear one where he’s talking about the economy. But some of his other favorite topics are the ballroom, the new construction of the helipad on the South Lawn. And among all the various controversies that Trump has, these are physical, tangible things that voters really latch on to that Trump loves to talk about. At his core, it’s, like, cool to be president, but he’s sort of more animated by being a developer, you know, and a construction magnate. And so when he is talking about the marbling or the gilding or the slope of the helipad, even though that has nothing to do with the economy, that’s sort of the problem. That reminds voters, Look, this guy is focused on things for himself and his rich friends that again have nothing to do with me . So Republicans privately will say, This is a nightmare . But at the end of the day, he’s their president, he’s what they’ve got. They know now, in sort of our 12th, 13th year of Trump, he’s not gonna change, and so this is the landscape they live in. Scherer: And the biggest issue right now is not what the president is saying; it’s what the president has done. He won election very clearly in ’24 on the idea that he would lower prices and sort of reverse the economic squeeze that had emerged under Biden. And if you go back to February, March, White House was saying, like, This is how we’re gonna message this. This is our plan: Gas prices are down; interest rates are down; homeownership’s more affordable; generally, prices, inflation is stabilizing and dipping down . All that’s been reversed by the Iran war. And so the biggest issue is not what the president’s saying or not saying. It’s that on Sunday night, the U.S. again had kinetic strikes against Iran. And we talked to a bunch of Republicans last week, and every one of them said, Well, it’s gonna be okay because we’re gonna have less actual violence in the Middle East over the next couple months . Every time another bomb goes off in the Middle East, it’s a hit to Republicans at this point. Parker: And which, by the way, Michael is talking about the president promising to lower prices. His other big promise was no more foreign wars, right? So the thing that is contributing to prices is another very clear broken promise. Harris: Well, I wanted to ask: What are hearing about the administration’s strategy, current strategy in the war, right? As you mentioned, Michael, the bombings resumed over the weekend. Are we actually trying to get out of this war, and how are Republicans up for reelection talking to their constituents about it? Scherer: What the White House and the political advisers want is basically a cease of violence right now for the next couple months. I mean, that’s their desire, and they want to keep squeezing the Iranians. The Iranians are not in a great position economically, so they can keep squeezing them. The problem is the Iranians have enormous leverage on Trump, as we’ve just been describing. And the Iranian position is: We control the Strait of Hormuz . The U.S. position is: You don’t control the Strait of Hormuz . So there’s, like, this deadlock at the center of the conflict. So every time, you know, the Iranians re-mine the Gulf or fire at another ship and the U.S. feels tempted to retaliate, it’s undermining the strategy the president has. And right now, the president doesn’t have control over that. Harris: When we come back, Ashley and Michael on the burgeoning trade war with Canada and the Democrats chances in the midterm elections. [ Music ] Harris: So, Ashley, we have this actual war with Iran, but we also have this developing trade war with Canada. And it feels like the culmination of something that Mark Carney, the prime minister of Canada, said in January at Davos about the ways that countries with smaller economies needed to start renegotiating and looking out for themselves a little bit more. And there’s been a lot of tension between him and President Trump. But I guess the thing that I keep coming back to with this trade war with Canada is: How did we end up back here? Why are we in this trade war with Canada? Parker: Well, it’s the South Park truism of “Blame Canada,” right? Like, it’s just an easy thing to know. I mean, Trump likes tariffs. That’s clear and that’s true. And he’s very frustrated with Canada, in part because, as he said, you know, on the one hand, he’s sort of ready to get to trade-war footing with our neighbor to the north, and on the other hand, he’d happily make Canada a 51st state. But therein is kind of the rub. If you hear Trump talk about it, he sort of says, Canada is getting all of the advantages of being a state, right? We’re subsidizing them to the tune of $200 billion . That’s not an accurate number, but that is what he says. And the thing that bothers Trump more than anything else is sort of, in his view, when people are taking advantage of him, profiting off of him. And, you know, that goes to, you know, former aides writing best-selling books from their time in the White House, to countries he believes sort of should be showing more deference to the United States than they are. And then on the flip side, you mentioned Mark Carney’s speech to Davos, where he said what we’ve been hearing publicly a bit, and especially privately from a lot of our other especially European allies, which is: Originally, after Trump’s first term, they sort of thought it was, like, a fever dream that they could PTSD black out when Biden returned to the scene. And I remember going on Biden’s first foreign trip—I can’t remember if it was like a G7 or a G20—but that was literally his message. I t was like, America, the America you know, the America you love; we’re back . And then when Trump came back to power, the view, especially from our allies, was like, Maybe Biden was the aberration , right? And even though we know, you know, allegedly Trump was not gonna run for a third term, like, the allies’ thinking is, We have no idea if a new Trump, if a J. D. Vance, or if a populist on the Democrats’ side is gonna come in. And we kind of have to—we can’t count on the U.S., and these tacit deals we used to make with the U.S. (and by that I don’t mean a trade deal, but sort of that, like, We show deference to the United States because they are a bigger, more powerful, and ultimately benevolent force in the world )— we’re willing to take that; we’re willing to subjugate ourselves a bit . They’ve decided, like, We’re not gonna do that anymore . So you also have a changing stance from our allies being much more willing to stand up for the United States and say, like, I’m not gonna bend my knee, because I can’t count on the United States. And by the way, I could agree to the worst trade terms with this president possible, and that might only placate him until his next Truth Social post . Harris: Yeah, you know, actually, to that point of sort of the deference that was shown, we’ve also seen the ways that the president has sort of out-and-out attacked allied nations in recent weeks, from South Korea, thinking about some of the threats towards places like Oman. And these aren’t small things, right? Even the fact that you mentioned something like the president saying that he’s not gonna run for a third term—to even to even think about a third term is sort of moving into an uncharted territory. Where does that leave the sort of long-term view of American responsibility as a world player? Scherer: I mean, I think everybody’s just waiting out Trump to see what happens next. And I think what you’ve seen in Canada is their conclusion. I mean, exactly how that fell apart is, you know, there’s conflicting stories. But it does seem pretty clear that Canada views its maximum point of leverage as being right now. I mean, if they threaten to withhold electricity from the United States before midterm elections, that obviously it could have huge impacts on Trump. If they threaten to withhold electricity in early January, when Trump’s a lame duck, it may not have the same import. I think the rest of the world is just coping with Trump. I mean, he’s so unpredictable. We don’t know how the last two years of his term will go. There’s just been a lot of preparation around the world to figure out how to reorient their own, you know, foreign policy to not depend on the U.S. going forward. Harris: Yeah, we’ve talked about Republicans. I want to talk about the Democrats for just a moment. And Ashley, you’ve done some reporting on the Democrats and how they’re thinking about the midterms. How much does the infighting of the primary, sort of the bitterness of the campaigns between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens in Michigan, races in Wisconsin, Florida, Maine, et cetera, sort of matter now to Democrats? And do Republicans sort of see an offset with the unpopularity of the president and the sort of discord that they might see among the Democrats? Parker: I mean, it’s not helpful, right? One thing, when you talk about these races and you talk to people on both sides, and it’s always true, it’s like it’s a national referendum, but at the end of the day, candidates matter, districts matter, the dynamics of states matter, right? And so, you know, Susan Collins is someone who has great name recognition in Maine, fits the state very well. I’ve talked to Democrats who don’t vote for her, but they’ve told me, they’ve been like, I have to say, she has amazing constituent services, right? You know, when I was DOGEd, like, she was in constant contact with me . And so, you know, for a state like that, or in Michigan, right, like, if you’re the Democrats, you want the best possible candidate for a general election. And there’s a sense among Democrats and Republicans that in some of these states and districts, they’ve done that, and in some of these states and districts, because of contentious primaries, they haven’t. That’s the first thing. And it’s interesting: Republicans in many ways should be doing even worse than they seem poised to do, and when you kind of drill down on that a bit, one of the things you hear is, at the end of the day, every election is a choice, right? And Democrats have a pretty bad brand, universally. Someone even said to me, Look, people don’t like the economy right now, what they’re feeling . And voters have short-term memories, but they still remember the Biden economy . And Democrats, again, individual candidates are doing things that are very compelling. But as a party, if I asked you, What is the Democratic Party plan to make this economic pinch better, to lower inflation, to cut prices? , almost no voter could tell you, because there doesn’t seem to be a bite-size talking point, cohesive, catchy, snappy Democratic plan. Harris: People have pushed back against sloganeering and things like that, but not having a sort of digestible plan, not sort of having that digestible slogan, can also be an issue for voters who don’t necessarily see the big picture, right? ’Cause if you say, Well, we have a policy for supplemental nutrition benefits, and then we also have a policy for this and for this , it doesn’t sort of capture an economic picture. So how much does that sloganeering matter? Parker: It’s Already I’m asleep , right? Harris: Yeah. Parker: I was talking to someone who runs focus groups among swing voters, and this person told me, You know, in a lot of these states, they will hold up the picture of the two Senate candidates running against each other in an election that’s now two months from now, and the voters can’t identify who either candidate is . And I don’t say that—I’m not making fun of voters. It’s a reality that like people are dealing with other things, right? Including the high cost. So if you don’t even know the names of the candidates, the idea that you’re gonna remember like the third policy platform of an economic plan, it has to be something that—and I get the sloganeering and this kind of cheesiness about that. But at the end of the day, one thing that President Trump is great at is getting people to sort of remember and understand what it is he ostensibly cares about, right? Whether that’s “Drain the Swamp” or Space Force. And Democrats need to find a way to signal—need an elevator pitch that voters can say, I’m voting for the Democrats because I know that my interest rate will go down to 3.875 percent . To dream. Harris: Yeah. Michael, Republicans have a lot of money going into this election. How are they spending it? Sort of putting the president’s TV ads aside, how are they currently spending that money, and will that have an effect, right? Will that matter? Scherer: Yeah, normally, the last decade or so, Democrats go into midterms, even they go into presidentials, with pretty substantial financial advantages. This is reversed this time. You know, by some estimates, if the president spent all the money he’s raised—and there’s a lot of dark money we can just estimate; we don’t really know—you’re talking about a $600 million to $1 billion advantage on the Republican side. We know there’ll be a couple hundred million that will be spent because these are in the congressional and the Senate committees and in the campaign committees. We don’t know what the president’s gonna spend. We know that they plan to spend something. We know some portion of what they spend will be on ads defending the president’s record. But, you know, the president said in a recent interview that he had, I think, $850 million. We don’t have that on documents; we don’t know if that’s true. But if that’s true and he decides to spend all of it, that could be enormously impactful in a race like this. I think it’s more likely he doesn’t spend all of it. I think the chance he can re-raise that amount of money in his last two years of office are pretty slim, and he probably wants to continue to have leverage over the party going forward, going into the next presidential race. So there’s a lot of speculation. What is also very clear is: They have not done the typical thing you do when you have a huge financial advantage, which is to go up early and spend money in the spring or, you know, even in the summer to sort of lay the groundwork when your opponents can’t afford to be up on the air, you kind of have the airwaves to yourself. They haven’t done that, really. So there’s a lot of suspense, I think, about how that’s actually going to play out in the final months. Harris: I’m gonna ask both of you to sort of open your reporter’s notebooks and think about sort of the threads that you’re going to be following this week. So, Ashley, I’m gonna go to you first. Sort of open your notebook. What are you thinking about in this week ahead? Parker: Sure, I mean, I alluded to it a bit before, but the bottom, by all accounts, should have fallen out for Republicans in this midterm cycle. Just the historical headwinds of a midterm election with an incumbent president, how that normally goes: An economic referendum when people feel the economy is not doing well; when the president and his party control the White House, both chambers of Congress; when voters don’t like the president’s approval numbers; and especially for this president in particular, who sort of sold himself not entirely accurately as a as a businessman; when his economic numbers are underwater for the first time. And so one thing I think Michael and I together are going to be looking at is—and again, it’s not that Republicans are supposed to do fantastically well, but there is a sense that, sort of generically, they should be doing worse than it looks like they’re going to be poised to do, which is: It looks like they’re probably gonna lose the House, lose their majority, but not by a ton. And the Senate is gonna be a real squeaker, which they may hold; Democrats may win, but it’ll be super tight. So trying to get into: Why are Republicans, even with gas prices what they are in August approaching an election, still sort of managing to barely hang on? Harris: And Michael, same question to you. Scherer: Another thing Ashley and I’ve been looking at is Cabinet travel. The president’s actually been—the White House’s been pretty good at deploying people around the country in a rather organized and sensible fashion. And then I’ve been working on a story about the sort of under-the-radar battle between the U.S. and Iran over decapitation assassination threats, which has sort of been, like, a weird current from the start of this conflict—where we started the war with Israel taking out most of the leadership of Iran, and continues now to, you know, there’s billboards all over Tehran now with the faces of the president’s family calling for their assassination, bounties on members of the administration and the family. So I’m looking at that as well. Harris: Well, there will be a lot to look at in the week and months ahead as we run up to the midterms. Thank you both for helping us understand it better, and thanks for joining the show today. Scherer: Yeah, thank you. Parker: Thank you for having us. [ Music ] Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli. It was edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic Audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, you can subscribe to Radio Atlantic on The Atlantic’ s YouTube page, on Apple, or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

items.title: Côte d’Ivoire: début de la campagne de cacao, la carte du producteur devient obligatoire
items.description: En Côte d’Ivoire, c’est ce mardi 1ᵉʳ septembre que s’ouvre la grande campagne de commercialisation du cacao avec l’annonce du nouveau prix bord champ du kilogramme de l’or brun ivoirien. items.title: Soudan: les préparatifs du dialogue national débutent sans les FSR
items.description: Au Soudan, les travaux pour un dialogue soudanais ont commencé. C’est ce qu’a annoncé, dimanche 30 juin, à Khartoum, le Comité de préparation du dialogue national, à l’issue de sa première réunion. Cette initiative a été annoncée par le commandant de l’armée, le général Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, mi-août. Selon lui, elle doit permettre au pays d’instaurer une paix durable, bien que le pays soit toujours en guerre et que les Forces de soutien rapide (FSR) que combat l’armée, depuis trois ans, ne soient pas conviées.

items.title: China, Kyrgyzstan agree to enhance cooperation in various fields
items.description: China and Kyrgyzstan have pledged to boost cooperation in various fields as both sides agree that bilateral ties are currently at their best in history, according to a joint declaration issued on Monday. In the document released during Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to the country, the two countries have agreed to make active efforts to ensure the safe implementation of strategic cooperation projects. Both sides have also agreed to actively promote cooperation in the financial sector, support eligible Kyrgyz banks in joining China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, and expand the use of local currencies in bilateral trade and investment settlement, said the declaration. China would expand market access for high-quality Kyrgyz agricultural products, it added. The two sides will ensure the smooth and timely implementation of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project, they said in the declaration. China welcomes Kyrgyzstan's participation in the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, it added. Both sides voiced opposition to all forms of unilateralism and protectionism, and called for the practice of true multilateralism. Kyrgyzstan reiterated its support for the one-China principle, as well as its opposition to all forms of "Taiwan independence," it said.

items.title: Xi says China to deepen comprehensive strategic partnership with Egypt
items.description: Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Tuesday that China stands ready to deepen its comprehensive strategic partnership with Egypt. Xi made the remarks in a signed article published in Egyptian media outlets ahead of his state visit to the country. In the article, Xi called on China and Egypt to enhance mutual trust and set an example of carrying forward friendship. The two sides should continue supporting each other on core interests and major concerns, and deepen exchanges and cooperation at various levels and across all sectors to ensure that the baton of friendship is passed on from generation to generation, he said. The two countries should pursue mutual benefit and win-win cooperation, and set a benchmark for joint development, Xi said. China and Egypt should forge greater synergy in development strategies, engage in high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, proactively tap the potential and expand the scope of pragmatic collaboration in a bid to provide sustained impetus to the mutually beneficial cooperation, he noted. He also urged the two sides to appreciate the beauty of each civilization and set an example for exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations. The two sides should deepen exchanges and cooperation in areas such as education, tourism, science and technology, health, sports and archaeology, forge a stronger bond of mutual understanding and affinity between the two peoples, with a view to injecting new momentum into the China-Egypt comprehensive strategic partnership, and harnessing the strengths of diverse civilizations to promote the building of a community with a shared future for humanity, he added. China and Egypt, Xi said, should move forward side by side, and be pioneers in upholding fairness and justice. As both major developing countries and important Global South nations, China and Egypt should vigorously uphold world peace and stability, and international fairness and justice by practicing true multilateralism, enhancing multilateral coordination, and working together to deliver on the four global initiatives on development, security, civilization and governance, he noted. The two countries should stand united and work together to steer China-Arab and China-Africa cooperation, Xi said, expressing China's readiness to work with the Egyptian side to enhance the demonstration effect of their well-established cooperation, leverage Egypt's unique location in linking the Arab world and reaching across the African continent, further implement the proposal on building "five cooperation frameworks" between China and Arab states and follow up on the ten partnership actions for modernization between China and Africa. This will ensure that China-Arab and China-Africa cooperation keeps pace with the times, makes steady progress and goes a long way, he added.

items.title: Le ministère de la santé s’apprête à mettre en service à Nouakchott 28 nouveaux centres de santé
items.description: Le ministère de la Santé a entamé les préparatifs de la dernière phase avant la mise en service d’un certain nombre de nouveaux centres de santé à Nouakchott, parmi les infrastructures réalisées dans le cadre du programme d’urgence pour le développement de la capitale. Dans ce contexte, le ministre de la Santé, Thiam Tidjani, a présidé lundi une réunion regroupant les directeurs régionaux de la santé et les médecins-chefs des trois wilayas de Nouakchott, afin d’examiner l’état de préparation de ces centres ainsi que leurs besoins en équipements et en personnel avant d’accueillir les citoyens. La réunion s’est principalement concentrée sur la détermination des besoins réels de chaque centre en médecins, infirmiers et personnel de santé, ainsi que sur le suivi de la mise en place des équipements et la mise en place d’un mécanisme de répartition des ressources humaines garantissant le lancement des services dans de bonnes conditions. Le ministre a appelé à une coordination des efforts entre les administrations centrales et les services régionaux, ainsi qu’à un suivi de près du processus de mise en service des nouveaux centres, afin qu’ils soient prêts à fournir leurs services dès leur ouverture. Le volet sanitaire du programme d’urgence pour le développement de Nouakchott comprend 28 établissements de santé répartis dans les neuf moughatas de la capitale, qu’il s’agisse de constructions, d’équipements ou de réhabilitations.

items.title: Campagne agricole humide dans le Nazinon : environ 340 000 tonnes de céréales attendues
items.description: La campagne agricole humide suit son cours dans toutes les localités du pays. A Tentenga et à Besim-Noghin, deux villages situés à l’Est de la commune de Manga, dans la région du Nazinon, les cultures affichent des niveaux d’évolution différents. Entre espoir d’une bonne récolte et inquiétudes liées à la pluviométrie, les producteurs restent mobilisés dans leurs champs. Constat ! Les champs verdissent progressivement dans les villages de Tentenga et de Besim-Noghin, situés à l’Est de la commune de Manga, dans la région du Nazinon. C’est le constat fait ce mercredi 26 août 2026, sur le site du bas-fond rizicole de Pologo, aménagé par le ministère en charge de l’agriculture. D’une superficie de 50 hectares, la rizière, située dans le village de Tentenga, est exploitée par la société coopérative des producteurs de riz dénommée : ‘’Namalgb-Zanga’’. Sur le périmètre irrigué, l’on y cultive essentiellement que du riz. Les jeunes plants y sont toujours au stade de tallage et du repiquage. « La saison de cette année ne ressemble pas à celle de l’année dernière. On est en retard à cause du démarrage tardif des pluies », a déploré le président de la société coopérative ‘’Namalgb-Zanga’’, Paul Nana. Selon lui, c’est à partir du mois d’août que la pluie s’est bien installée. Et là également, a-t-il souligné, il pleut tous les jours au point que l’on n’arrive pas à travailler sur les parcelles. Paul Nana. « S’il pleut jusqu’en fin octobre, les récoltes seront bonnes », a-t-il dit. Le président de la société coopérative ‘’Namalgb-Zanga’’ a affirmé également avoir reçu des semences, de labours gratuits et de l’engrais des services de l’agriculture. « Nous recevons régulièrement des visites et des appuis-conseils des techniciens agricoles », a salué Paul Nana avant d’ajouter que ces initiatives leur permettent de corriger les imperfections et d’améliorer leurs cultures. Sur les parcelles de la société coopérative ‘’Nabonswendé’’, situées dans le village de Besim-Noghin, les cultures présentent une bonne physionomie. Elles sont au stade d’épiaison. Sur ce site de 20 hectares, emblavé par le ministère en charge de l’agriculture, plusieurs spéculations sont cultivées. Il s’agit, notamment du riz, du petit mil et du maïs. Malgré le démarrage tardif des pluies, le vice-président de la société coopérative ‘’Nabonswendé’’, Issiaka Tiemtoré, a dit rendre grâce à Dieu. « Environ 2 100 hectares de labours réalisés » Le riz est à l’étape d’épiaison sur le site du bas-fond de Besim-Noghin. " data-large-file="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-1.png" class="size-medium wp-image-168554" src="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-1-300x200.png" alt="" width="300" height="200" srcset="https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-1-300x200.png 300w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-1-768x512.png 768w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-1-630x420.png 630w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-1-150x100.png 150w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-1-696x464.png 696w, https://www.sidwaya.info/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3-1.png 800w" sizes="(max-width: 300px) 100vw, 300px" /> Le riz est à l’étape d’épiaison sur le site du bas-fond de Besim-Noghin. Il a dit avoir commencé les cultures dès les premières pluies. « Nous avons suivi les conseils des services agricoles. Lorsque nous avons reçus les semences, ils nous ont dit de commencer très tôt », a indiqué M. Tiemtoré. Le directeur régional chargé de l’agriculture du Nazinon, Honoré Onadja, a signifié que la campagne humide dans sa circonscription administrative s’est bien installée. « De manière générale, la situation est satisfaisante dans la région », a-t-il laissé entendre. Selon lui, il est vrai que l’installation de la saison a été tardive mais les quantités d’eaux reçues actuellement sont suffisantes pour couvrir les besoins des plantes. Honoré Onadja a indiqué que pour la campagne agricole, sa structure a fixé des objectifs de production qui couvrent plusieurs cultures. A titre illustratif, pour les céréales, a-t-il confié, l’objectif régional est d’environ 340 000 tonnes, avec une place importante accordée au maïs, au riz, au sorgho et au mil. « Nous visons également environ 91 500 tonnes de cultures de rente, notamment l’arachide, le sésame et le soja ainsi qu’environ 59 700 tonnes d’autres cultures vivrières, avec une place importante pour le niébé et le voandzou », a précisé le directeur régional chargé de l’agriculture du Nazinon. En ce qui concerne les appuis de la campagne, il a relevé que des intrants agricoles ont été mis à la disposition des producteurs. A cet effet, Honoré Onadja, a cité des semences de variétés améliorées, des engrais minéraux, de la fumure organique et des pesticides. Il a par ailleurs fait savoir que cinq tracteurs ont été mobilisés au cours de la campagne ayant permis de réaliser environ 2 100 hectares de labours. Le premier responsable de l’agriculture du Nazinon a pour l’occasion invité les agriculteurs à maintenir les opérations d’entretien des plantes, à poursuivre la surveillance des parcelles et à signaler rapidement toute difficulté aux services techniques de sa structure. Noufou SAWADOGO

items.title: Kagbelen : un accident de circulation fait une vingtaine de blessés et d’importants dégâts matériels
items.description: Un grave accident de la circulation s’est produit ce lundi 31 août 2026 à Kagbelen-Village, dans la commune urbaine de Kagbelen, précisément à l’endroit où le train de Rusal avait déraillé. L’accident a fait état d’une vingtaine de blessés et causé d’importants dégâts matériels, entraînant un embouteillage considérable sur l’axe. Selon plusieurs témoins présents sur les lieux, l’accident a impliqué un gros camion qui aurait subitement perdu le contrôle de ses freins avant de percuter plusieurs véhicules. Au total, sept véhicules auraient été impliqués, dont trois fortement endommagés. Plusieurs passagers se trouvant à bord des véhicules ont été blessés dans la collision. Aboubacar Camara, membre du syndicat de Kagbelen, explique avoir été alerté peu après le départ des véhicules qu’il avait embarqués. > « J’ai reçu un appel m’informant de l’accident. Je me suis immédiatement rendu sur les lieux pour constater les faits. Effectivement, il y avait eu un accident », a-t-il déclaré. Parmi les victimes, Aboubacar Soumah, blessé notamment, au niveau du bras, a raconté les circonstances de l’accident. Il affirme qu’il se rendait à Dubréka lorsqu’il a aperçu au loin le camion qui semblait avoir perdu le contrôle. > « Nous avons aperçu le camion de loin, mais il était déjà sans contrôle. Finalement, notre véhicule a été percuté et renversé dans un fossé. Plusieurs personnes ont été blessées et il y a eu d’importants dégâts matériels », a témoigné la victime. Mobilisés autour des blessés, les secouristes de la Croix-Rouge communale de Kagbelen ont déploré l’ampleur de l’accident. À leur arrivée sur les lieux, plusieurs blessés ont été pris en charge et orientés vers l’hôpital préfectoral de Dubréka, afin de recevoir des soins. L’accident a également provoqué un important ralentissement de la circulation. Au moment où nous quittions les lieux, un embouteillage de grande ampleur paralysait complètement la circulation sur cet axe très fréquenté. Les circonstances exactes de l’accident ainsi que le bilan définitif des victimes restent à préciser.

items.title: Le ministère de l’hydraulique affirme que la production d’eau pour Nouakchott est demeurée normale malgré la forte turbidité des eaux du fleuve
items.description: Le ministère de l'hydraulique a déclaré que le système d'Aftout Sahli avait maintenu ses niveaux normaux de production d'eau destinée à la ville de Nouakchott, malgré la forte turbidité dans les eaux du fleuve au cours des dernières semaines. Le ministère a ajouté dans un communiqué que le niveau de turbidité à la prise d’eau du réseau avait dépassé le seuil des 1 000 unités depuis le 21 juillet dernier et s’était maintenu à des niveaux élevés jusqu’à la fin du mois d’août, période généralement considérée comme l’une des plus chargées en turbidité de l’année. Il a indiqué que le réseau avait enregistré son niveau de turbidité le plus élevé de l’année en cours le 8 août 2026, avec 4 568 unités NTU, avant de se stabiliser ces derniers jours à des niveaux élevés, le dernier en date s’élevant à 1 780 unités. Malgré ces conditions, la production du réseau s’est maintenue à ses niveaux habituels, oscillant entre 147 000 et 150 000 mètres cubes par jour, ce qui correspond à la capacité maximale de production.

items.title: Dr Sandrine Ouédraogo, chirurgienne-dentiste : « La mauvaise haleine peut être un facteur de répercussion psychologique sur les relations professionnelles et sociales »
items.description: Fréquente chez les personnes ayant une mauvaise santé bucco-dentaire, une bouche sèche, les fumeurs et consommateurs d’alcool, la mauvaise haleine conduit le plus souvent le patient à la perte d’estime de soi et la solitude. La chirurgienne-dentiste, Dr Sandrine Ouédraogo explique comment éviter la mauvaise haleine et prévenir ses conséquences psychologique et sociale. Sidwaya (S) : Qu’est qu’une mauvaise haleine ? Dr Sandrine Ouédraogo (S.O) : La mauvaise haleine ou « halitose » en terme médical, est une odeur désagréable et incommodante provenant de la bouche et parfois du nez, lorsque nous parlons ou respirons. De façon simple, on dira que la mauvaise haleine est une bouche qui sent mauvais. S : Quelles sont les causes de cette mauvaise haleine chez les patients ? S.O : Les causes de l’halitose sont multiples : nous avons les causes locales et les causes d’ordre général. En ce qui concerne les causes locales, elles peuvent être due à la mauvaise hygiène bucco-dentaire, la plaque dentaire, le tartre, les caries dentaires, l’abcès, les maladies de la gencive, c’est-à-dire la gingivite, les maladies des tissus de soutiens de la dent comme la parodontite, la sécheresse buccale provoquée par des médicaments, un jeûne prolongé ou quand la bouche reste fermée pendant longtemps. Pour les causes générales, nous avons des causes ORL telles que les otites, les amygdalites avec le caséum, les sinusites, les rhinites. La mauvaise haleine a aussi des causes gastriques telles que le reflux gastro-œsophagien (remontés acides), les ulcères. A cela, s’ajoutent d’autres maladies telles que le diabète, les maladies rénales, les maladies hépatiques (…). En dehors de ces causes, il y a le stress qui peut provoquer une mauvaise haleine. La mauvaise haleine n’est pas héréditaire mais certaines habitudes familiales peuvent influencer son apparition. Elle peut être également d’origine alimentaire. S : Quels sont les aliments qui sont les plus à l’origine d’une mauvaise haleine ? S.O : Ce sont des aliments contenants des composés sulfurés volatils comme l’ail, les oignons, certains aliments épicés, la viande, le fromage (…). Il y a aussi l’alcool, le tabac. Toutefois, La mauvaise haleine d’origine alimentaire est passagère. S : Quels sont les cas ou degrés de mauvaise haleine que vous rencontrez au quotidien chez les patients ? S.O : Il n’y a pas de classification type, mais certains auteurs ont tenté de faire une classification selon le degré des odeurs. Il y a l’absence totale d’odeur perceptible, l’odeur à peine perceptible, l’odeur légère mais bien reconnaissable, l’odeur modérée mais clairement incommodante, l’odeur forte, très désagréable et insupportable. Nous avons également l’halitophobie qui est la peur constante d’avoir une mauvaise haleine, alors qu’il n’en est rien. S : Est-ce que la mauvaise haleine a des conséquences sur la santé humaine ? S.O : La mauvaise haleine a principalement des répercussions psychologiques sur la personne qui aura tendance à s’isoler, à perdre confiance en lui, et être anxieux. La personne ayant une mauvaise haleine peut être stigmatisée par ses proches, ce qui entraînera des conséquences sur ses relations professionnelles et sociales. Il faut noter aussi que la mauvaise haleine est surtout un symptôme, un signe qui peut traduire un problème sous-jacent. Donc elle ne va pas entrainer les maladies en question mais peut signifier qu’une maladie existe, d’où la nécessité à se faire consulter par un professionnel de la santé bucco-dentaire. S : Quelles sont les précautions à prendre lorsqu’on constate une mauvaise haleine ? S.O : Quand vous constatez une mauvaise haleine, il faut d’abord renforcer votre hygiène bucco-dentaire. Ensuite, boire suffisamment d’eau. Lorsque la mauvaise haleine est chronique, il faut consulter un chirurgien-dentiste pour rechercher les causes. Celui-ci va faire une remise en état de la bouche. Si ça persiste ou si la cause n’est pas d’origine dentaire, il va vous référer chez un médecin ORL ou un gastro-entérologue. Tant que la cause n’est pas prise en charge, la mauvaise haleine va continuer. Si la cause est identifiée et traitée, le patient peut définitivement venir à bout de la mauvaise haleine. S : Quels sont les types de produits utilisés ou à éviter lorsqu’on a une mauvaise haleine ? S.O : Vous pouvez utiliser du dentifrice fluoré, des bains de bouches fluorés, des chewing-gum non sucrés sans abuser pour activer la salivation, des pastilles mentholées, des feuilles de menthe, les fils dentaires et les brossettes interdentaires. Il faut éviter les bains de bouche contenant de l’alcool, bonbons et chewing-gums très sucrés, remèdes maisons agressifs, ainsi que les médicaments qui ne sont pas prescrits. S : Quelles sont les bonnes pratiques pour ne pas avoir une mauvaise haleine ? S.O : Pour ne pas avoir une mauvaise haleine, il faut avoir une bonne hygiène bucco-dentaire en se brossant bien les dents 2 fois par jour après les repas, on brosse de la gencive vers la dent, on brosse toutes les dents et toutes les faces des dents, sans oublier la langue. Compléter le brossage avec du fil dentaire ou des brossettes interdentaires et changer la brosse à dent tous les 3 mois ou avant 3 mois, si celle-ci est abîmée. Eviter la consommation du tabac et d’alcool, boire beaucoup d’eau environ 1,5 à 2 l d’eau par jour pour les adultes. Consulter régulièrement un chirurgien-dentiste au moins une fois par an, même en l’absence de douleur, pour contrôler ses dents et les soigner s’il y a des problèmes. S : Un conseil à l’endroit des proches des personnes qui souffrent de ce mal S.O : Lorsque l’un de vos proches à une mauvaise haleine persistante, il est important de trouver une manière bienveillante et respectueuse de lui en parler, sans ne le frustrer ni l’isoler. En effet, certaines personnes peuvent ne pas savoir qu’elles ont une mauvaise haleine. D’autres en sont conscientes, mais n’ont peut-être pas encore trouvé de solution et, dans ce cas, elles souffrent déjà suffisamment de cette situation. Pour les personnes qui en souffrent, je dirais que la mauvaise haleine n’est pas une fatalité, elle peut être prise en charge et se soigner. S : Quel est le service qui s’occupe des patients souffrant d’une mauvaise haleine ? S.O : La prise en charge de l’halitose peut être pluridisciplinaire, c’est-à-dire plusieurs services. D’une part il y a le service d’odonto-stomatologie ou service de chirurgie dentaire ou cabinet dentaire. D’autre part, les services d’ORL et de gastro-entérologie en fonction des cas. Interview réalisée par Gbetcheni Constantin Bertrand KAMBIRE (Collaborateur)

Le parti au pouvoir Insaf qualifie de grand succès les tournées organisées par ses missions dans 5 wilayas du pays
items.description: Le Parti politique au pouvoir en Mauritanie, Insaf, a déclaré ce lundi que les tournées sur le terrain organisées dans cinq wilayas ces derniers temps avaient remporté un « grand succès », précisant qu'elles comprenaient des réunions politiques et organisationnelles, des festivals ainsi que des rencontres avec ses instances, ses élus, ses cadres, ses personnalités, ses acteurs politiques et ses militants. Dans un communiqué publié à l’issue d’une réunion entre son président, Mohamed Ould Bilal Messaoud, et les secrétaires permanents chargés des wilayas, le parti a précisé que ces tournées avaient couvert les wilayas d’Inchiri, de l’Adrar, du Tagant, de l’Assaba et du Hodh Chargui, et que les différentes étapes avaient donné lieu à des réceptions ainsi qu’à des festivals régionaux et départementaux. La réunion a permis de passer en revue les rapports des visites sur le terrain ainsi que les observations, préoccupations et propositions qu’ils contenaient. Le président du parti a appelé à étudier et analyser ces questions, à s’attacher à y remédier et à rechercher des solutions possibles en coordination avec les instances concernées. Le parti a déclaré que cela visait à faire de ces tournées un outil permettant d’identifier les préoccupations des citoyens, d’en assurer le suivi et d’y répondre, tout en améliorant les performances du parti et en renforçant sa présence sur le terrain. Ces tournées ont couvert les moughatas d’Akjoujt et de Benichab dans l’Inchiri, d’Atar, de Chinguetti, de Ouadane et d’Aoujeft dans l’Adrar, de Tidjikja, de Tichit et de Moudjéria dans le Tagant, ainsi que celles de Kiffa, de Kankossa, de Guérou, de Boumdeid et de Barkéol dans l’Assaba, ainsi que Nema, Walata, N’Beïket, Lahouach, Bassiknou, Adel Begrou, Amourj, Djiguenni et Timbédra dans le Hodh Chargui. Le parti a exprimé sa gratitude envers les instances du parti, les élus, les cadres, les personnalités, les acteurs politiques et les militants pour ce qu’il a qualifié d’efforts déployés afin d’organiser et d’assurer le succès des différentes étapes de la tournée. Il a déclaré que les interventions et les communiqués publiés par ses militants au cours de ces visites ont mis en avant les acquis de la présidence de Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani et exprimé le souhait de poursuivre sur la voie des réformes, du développement et de la stabilité, selon le communiqué. À l’issue de la réunion, le président du parti a appelé les secrétaires permanents et les instances du parti à tirer parti de ce qu’il a qualifié d’élan politique et populaire manifesté lors des tournées, à continuer d’expliquer le discours du parti, à faire connaître ce qu’il a qualifié de bilan des réalisations et à renforcer la mobilisation autour du programme de développement du président.
